interactions.label: An intern prescribes '100 g rice' to provide approximately 350 kcal in a child's

params.question: An intern prescribes '100 g rice' to provide approximately 350 kcal in a child's meal plan. The mother serves 100 g of cooked rice. Which statement best explains the resulting caloric shortfall?

answers.text: There is no shortfall — 100 g of cooked rice provides approximately 350 kcal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. 100 g of cooked rice provides only about 130–145 kcal, not 350 kcal. The raw-vs-cooked distinction matters greatly in dietary prescriptions.

answers.text: Rice loses most of its caloric value during cooking because starch is broken down by heat

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Starch is not destroyed by cooking — the calories per gram of rice solids remain similar. The reduction in caloric density per 100 g of cooked rice is due to water absorption, which roughly triples the weight.

answers.text: 100 g of raw rice provides 345–360 kcal, but cooking triples the weight with water, so 100 g of cooked rice yields only ~130–145 kcal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cooking rice absorbs water and approximately triples its weight, reducing the caloric density per 100 g from 345–360 kcal (raw) to about 130–145 kcal (cooked).

answers.text: The shortfall exists because the mother should have used parboiled rice, which retains its full caloric value after cooking

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. All varieties of rice absorb water during cooking and show a similar reduction in caloric density per unit cooked weight. The issue is specifying raw vs cooked weight, not the rice variety.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key point: cooking rice adds water and triples its weight. 100 g of raw rice (345–360 kcal) becomes ~300 g of cooked rice. So 100 g of cooked rice provides only ~130–145 kcal — less than half the intended 350 kcal. This raw-vs-cooked distinction is a common source of error in dietary prescriptions.

Correct. Always specify 'raw weight' or 'cooked weight' when prescribing cereal quantities in a diet plan. Raw rice (345–360 kcal/100g) yields about three times its weight when cooked, reducing caloric density to ~130–145 kcal/100g.

interactions.label: In marasmus, the child shows severe wasting with loss of subcutaneous fat, while

params.question: In marasmus, the child shows severe wasting with loss of subcutaneous fat, while in kwashiorkor, subcutaneous fat is relatively preserved despite severe malnutrition. Which of the following best explains this clinical difference?

answers.text: Kwashiorkor is a milder form of malnutrition with less overall nutrient deficit than marasmus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Kwashiorkor is NOT milder — it is a form of SAM with its own life-threatening complications including hepatic steatosis, severe infections, and electrolyte disturbances.

answers.text: In marasmus, total energy-protein deficit drives catabolism of fat and muscle; in kwashiorkor, predominant protein deficit impairs albumin synthesis, causing oedema while fat stores are relatively spared

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Marasmus results from chronic total energy-protein deficiency — the body catabolises both fat and muscle to fuel vital organs. In kwashiorkor, predominantly protein-deficient diets impair albumin synthesis, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and causing oedema, while partial energy intake may preserve some fat stores.

answers.text: Children with kwashiorkor have a genetic resistance to lipolysis that prevents fat breakdown

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. There is no genetic fat-catabolism resistance in kwashiorkor. The difference lies in the type of nutritional deficit — total energy-protein deprivation (marasmus) vs predominant protein deficiency (kwashiorkor).

answers.text: Marasmus affects older children with higher metabolic rates, leading to more rapid fat depletion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Marasmus can affect any age group. The clinical difference relates to the nature of the dietary deficit (total vs predominantly protein), not the child's age or metabolic rate.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key concept: marasmus results from total energy-protein deficit — the body catabolises its own fat and muscle stores, producing severe wasting ('old-man face', 'baggy trousers'). Kwashiorkor results from predominant protein deficit — impaired albumin synthesis reduces plasma oncotic pressure, causing oedema, while some fat stores are preserved because energy intake is partially maintained.

Correct. The clinical distinction reflects the underlying nutritional deficit: marasmus (total energy-protein deprivation) causes catabolism of both fat and muscle, producing visible wasting. Kwashiorkor (predominant protein deficit) impairs albumin synthesis — the resulting hypoalbuminaemia reduces oncotic pressure, causing bilateral pitting oedema while some subcutaneous fat is preserved.

interactions.label: After puberty, sex-based differences in daily energy requirements narrow because

params.question: After puberty, sex-based differences in daily energy requirements narrow because both boys and girls reach similar lean body mass.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. After puberty, energy requirement differences between boys and girls WIDEN, not narrow. Testosterone drives greater lean body mass accrual in boys — muscle is more metabolically active than adipose tissue — so boys require substantially more energy (ICMR-NIN 2020: 16–18 years — boys ~2640 kcal/day vs girls ~2060 kcal/day).
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. After puberty, sex-based energy requirement differences actually WIDEN. Boys accumulate substantially more lean body mass (muscle) under androgenic influence, which is more metabolically active than adipose tissue, driving higher energy needs (ICMR-NIN 2020: 16–18 years — boys ~2640 kcal/day vs girls ~2060 kcal/day).

interactions.label: During the examination of a 12-year-old obese boy, an intern records only the we

params.question: During the examination of a 12-year-old obese boy, an intern records only the weight, height, and BMI, then plans to order blood investigations. Which critical assessment has the intern most likely omitted?

answers.text: Mid-upper arm circumference measurement for malnutrition screening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MUAC is a screening tool for undernutrition (SAM/MAM), not a key component of the obesity examination. The obesity exam has its own specific assessment priorities.

answers.text: Plotting height on a growth velocity chart to detect growth hormone deficiency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While height velocity may be relevant when suspecting secondary (endocrine) obesity, the most commonly omitted steps in a primary obesity examination are waist circumference, blood pressure, and skin marker assessments.

answers.text: Measuring blood pressure, waist circumference, and identifying cutaneous markers such as acanthosis nigricans

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These are the most commonly omitted yet clinically significant steps. Acanthosis nigricans indicates insulin resistance, raised blood pressure signals early cardiovascular risk, and waist circumference quantifies central adiposity — all carry immediate clinical implications.

answers.text: Performing a full neurological examination to exclude hypothalamic obesity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A full neurological exam is indicated when secondary obesity is suspected (e.g. headache, visual changes, short stature), but secondary causes account for less than 5% of childhood obesity. The commonly omitted assessments are blood pressure, waist circumference, and cutaneous markers.

overallFeedback.feedback: Stopping at weight, height, and BMI is a common clinical error highlighted in this segment. The obesity examination must also include: blood pressure measurement (often elevated), waist circumference or waist-hip ratio (central adiposity marker), and a structured search for cutaneous markers — acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance), striae, and pseudogynaecomastia — each with direct clinical implications.

Correct. The physical examination of an obese child must go beyond weight, height, and BMI. Blood pressure (early cardiovascular risk), waist circumference or waist-hip ratio (central adiposity), and cutaneous markers — acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance), striae, pseudogynaecomastia — are the assessments most commonly omitted by trainees yet carry the most immediate clinical significance.
